subtopic: Rituals and belonging
passage: On Lalit's first morning as the new teacher at the village middle school, the six staff sat on the veranda mat with steel cups of tea. Ritu, the headmistress, handed Lalit a cup and a piece of jaggery. “On a newcomer's first Monday, everyone says one thing they like about this school,” she said. The old maths teacher grinned and said, “The breeze.” The clerk said, “The children's singing.” The science teacher said nothing and only sipped. Lalit's shoulders had been tight since the bus ride. Ritu added, “It's not a test. We just want you to know how we start. Tomorrow you needn't bring anything.” Lalit smiled and said, “The bell that rings a little late,” and everybody laughed.

passage: On Wanjiru's first Friday in the Toronto lab, at four o'clock everybody drifted toward the meeting table. A cake sat in the middle. Xin, the senior scientist, said, “The new person picks next week's cake, and everyone shares one good thing from the week. You're allowed to pass.” A postdoc, Dan, said his experiment finally ran. Xin leaned over. “We started this so new people wouldn't have to guess how things work here. Next Friday it's yours to choose.” Wanjiru relaxed and asked what flavours people liked.

passage: Aiko had started her blog about the university's bike-lane debate to explain both sides. Her early posts got a few polite comments. Bidisha's diary, Tuesday night.
Banned from the film-club group today. Three thousand members, and one message from Sachin, the moderator: “Third spoiler warning ignored. You are removed.” I was so angry my hands shook. I had posted a spoiler as a joke, then argued with him in the thread while other people liked his replies. Nobody stood up for me. My first thought was that they're all petty. My second, a bit ashamed, was that the rule was fair and I did break it three times. And under all that, strangely, a small relief: I'll get my evenings back. Still, I used to check that group every morning. Tomorrow I'll go to the coffee shop and see if any of the real-life regulars are around.
Bidisha

passage: At eleven at night the birdwatchers' forum went down, and Varun, the volunteer moderator, sat at the kitchen table with cold tea and two hundred angry notifications. passage: Two days before her final exam, Jasleen's phone kept lighting up with the gaming clan's arguments: forty people calling one member “trash” and demanding a side. Her stomach felt tight, and her revision notes stayed unread. Shreya, from her study group, sent a message: “Coming to the library at four?” Jasleen looked at the clan chat, then at her cluttered desk. She typed, “I'm leaving. Good luck to all,” and pressed leave before she could change her mind. The chat went silent for a moment, then someone wrote, “Traitor.” Jasleen put the phone in a drawer and went to the library. Shreya slid over a coffee. “Proud of you,” Shreya whispered.

qa.q: How many people were arguing in the gaming clan?
qa.a: Forty people were arguing in the gaming clan.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling as the clan's arguments kept lighting up the phone?
qa.a: Jasleen felt tense and anxious, with a tight stomach, and could not concentrate on revision.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen make, and what helped keep it?
qa.a: Jasleen typed a polite goodbye and pressed leave, then put the phone in a drawer and went to the library, where Shreya's message and coffee kept the friendship going.

qa.q: How might the clan member who was called “trash” have seen Jasleen's leaving?
qa.a: That member may have felt more alone after Jasleen left, or may have felt relieved that someone stopped taking part in the pile-on.

grounding: A person notices a group leaves them anxious, steps away and keeps in touch with the study group, choosing peace over the group's approval.
